To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
lactic or acetric acid treatments were more effective at removing fecal contamination from prechilled beef carcass surfaces than trimming or washing with water.
lactic and acetic acid treatments were effective for the removal of pathogens from prechilled beef carcass surfaces.
lactic acid was the best decontamination agent for reducing E. coli O.157:H7 on beef carcass surface regions and that the inside round region was most resistant to decontamination.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a rapid and efficient method to reduce fecal contamination on beef carcass surfaces.
the development of methods for the removal of microbial contaminants from beef carcass surface regions and the reduction of microbial contamination spread.
the development of a model to predict microbial contamination levels on beef carcass surface regions after fecal contamination.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
all of these methods are effective for decontamination, but some methods are more effective than others, depending on the carcass region and type of pathogen being tested.

the most effective decontamination of beef carcass surfaces from fecal contamination can be achieved with organic acid treatment following a water wash, and this treatment should be applied to the inside round carcass region.
the use of organic acid washes in combination with mechanical removal of visible fecal contamination is an effective method of reducing the levels of fecal contamination of beef carcass surfaces.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the most effective treatment for decontaminating beef carcass surfaces is a combination of trimming and washing followed by organic acid application.
organic acid washes are effective for reducing levels of pathogens on beef carcass surfaces, but the effectiveness of the treatments is affected by carcass region and the pathogen.
the most effective treatment for reducing pathogen levels was washing with water followed by spraying with lactic acid.
The main takeaway from our work is that
decontamination methods that are used in the beef industry should be tailored to the carcass surface region being treated, because decontamination efficacy varies by carcass region.

organic acid treatments are more effective than water alone in reducing pathogen levels from carcass surface regions and that the use of organic acids is an effective means of reducing the risk of cross-contamination from carcass surfaces.
the most important factor affecting decontamination of beef carcass surfaces is carcass surface location.
